analysis.one_liner: Lets homeowners facing foreclosure stay in their homes as paying renters for up to 20 years.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote, one of many foreclosure-relief proposals introduced in 2008 as the housing crisis accelerated.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let homeowners facing foreclosure on a below-median-price home they had lived in for at least two years choose to stay put as renters for up to 20 years, paying a court-set fair market rent each month. The lender could still foreclose and sell the property, but the new owner would have to accept the former owner as a tenant, and could only evict for breaking the lease terms. It applied to foreclosures already underway and covered new ones for five years.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners in foreclosure on modest homes — a first mortgage on a single-family property bought below the area's median purchase price, used as their main residence for two years, and taken out before July 2007. Instead of losing their home outright, they could elect to remain as month-to-month tenants paying fair market rent, with protection from at-will eviction for the full 20-year period and annual rent adjustments tied to the consumer price index.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Owners of modest homes facing foreclosure

how_it_helps.text: Gives the homeowner the sole option to stay in the home for a 20-year tenancy after foreclosure, as long as they pay fair market rent and keep it as their principal residence [S3].
Requires the foreclosing creditor to give 28 days' written notice explaining the default and the right to rent before starting foreclosure, and bars foreclosure from starting earlier [S3].
Sets rent by a court-appointed independent appraiser, adjusts it annually with the CPI owners'-equivalent-rent index, and lets either party request a redetermination after 12 months [S3].

Does not block foreclosure or sale — the creditor keeps the right to foreclose and sell; the buyer simply takes title subject to the leasehold, and the homeowner keeps any existing right to reinstate the mortgage [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and whoever buys the foreclosed property. The creditor can still foreclose and sell, but the new owner cannot take possession for up to 20 years while the former owner pays rent. That ties up the property's value and possession, which lowers what the creditor can recover and would likely be priced into mortgage terms for borrowers generally.

drawbacks.text: A 20-year leasehold after foreclosure sharply reduces the value of a foreclosed property, because a buyer could not use or resell it for two decades while collecting only rent — lenders would recover far less on defaulted loans [S3].

Applying the law retroactively to foreclosures already in progress, and letting the occupant remove rent disputes to federal court, adds cost and uncertainty for creditors handling millions of 2008-era defaults [S3].

The cost of not regaining possession would not stop with lenders; it would plausibly surface as tighter credit or higher rates for future homebuyers, including the moderate-income buyers the bill aims to protect [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families on the edge of eviction in 2008, the guarantee of staying in the home as a paying tenant was a real, substantial benefit. The design is workable — rent is market-based, the creditor's foreclosure and sale rights are untouched, and the benefit is limited to modest homes and a five-year window. But the cost side is real: a 20-year claim on a foreclosed property is an unusually long encumbrance, and investors would discount foreclosed home values accordingly. It was a targeted, but expensive, form of foreclosure relief.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the Saving Family Homes Act of 2008 on May 21, 2008, with two Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day [S5].
No further action was ever taken; it never left committee and expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and foreclosure-sale investors kept the rules as they were — full right to possession after foreclosure — while roughly 2.3 million homes entered foreclosure during 2008. The homeowners the bill would have protected got nothing from it.

for.name: Rep. Raúl Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assigned it to the Financial Services Committee.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of referral (Rep. Barney Frank, D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after referral; it received no action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Democrats were involved on the support side and the bill never advanced far enough to draw recorded opposition, so no roll-call or floor split exists to measure the parties against each other.

industries.note: The bill would have cost lenders part of their recovery on defaulted loans by letting former owners occupy the property for up to 20 years at market rent. Lenders would bear that loss and would pass it on through credit terms.

Anyone buying a foreclosed home — including buyers of mortgage-backed securities — would take title subject to a two-decade leasehold, cutting the property's resale value and access. Foreclosed homes were a large asset class in 2008.
